query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The premelting and melting behavior of equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy (HEA) nanoparticles is governed by nanoscale surface chemical heterogeneity—specifically, preferential Cu segregation to the particle surface—which locally depresses the melting point and broadens the overall melting transition relative to a chemically homogeneous particle.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles (5–20 nm diameter).
generation.intervention: Compare two HEA nanoparticle ensembles: (1) as‐synthesized equiatomic particles with randomized alloying, and (2) identical particles subjected to a surface‐enrichment treatment that increases Cu concentration in the outer 1–2 nm shell.
generation.conditions: In‐situ heating from room temperature up to above the bulk HEA melting point (e.g., 300–1500 K) under vacuum in a transmission electron microscope (TEM) or differential scanning calorimeter (DSC) with heating rates of 5 K/min.
generation.structural_mediator: Degree of Cu surface segregation (atomic % Cu in the outermost 1–2 nm shell).
generation.mechanism: Localized Cu enrichment at the surface lowers the Gibbs free energy for surface disordering and nucleation of a premelted layer, so that surface‐driven melting initiates at lower temperature and proceeds over a broader range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Particles with enhanced surface Cu will exhibit a surface premelting onset at a lower temperature (by tens of kelvins) and a broader melting interval than the baseline (randomized) HEA particles.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic HEA nanoparticles with a randomized, homogeneous elemental distribution.
generation.boundary: Applies to HEA nanoparticles with diameters between ~5 nm and ~20 nm and equiatomic overall composition; may not hold for particles >20 nm or with heavy surface oxidation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the melting‐point depression and broadening (tens vs. hundreds of kelvins) is uncertain due to unknown equilibrium segregation levels and kinetics.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two matched sets of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles (5–20 nm): one set with no post‐treatment (randomized) and one set with a mild anneal reducing agent exposure to induce surface Cu segregation. Perform in‐situ TEM heating with real‐time diffraction to detect onset of surface disordering, and DSC to record melting peaks under identical heating rates.
measurements: Temperature of first detectable premelting (from diffraction peak broadening)
Onset and peak temperatures in DSC endotherm
High‐resolution STEM‐EDS line profiles to quantify surface Cu concentration
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both ensembles show identical premelting onset and melting peak temperatures within instrumental resolution (±10 K) despite significant differences in measured surface Cu concentration (>5 atomic %), then the hypothesis is falsified.
